description: We are passionate students from Uzbekistan with strong backgrounds in competitive programming, algorithms, and problem-solving. We’re interested in AI, software development, space exploration, and educational technology. Our goal is to build an engaging game that simulates managing a lunar or Martian outpost. We’re looking for creative teammates skilled in game development, UI/UX design, 3D modeling, space science, or frontend development. Let’s build something impactful together!
summary: A solar particle storm is coming. Your crew has already covered the lunar shelter with soil. There is one unit of power left. Do you run the air fan or switch on the greenhouse lights? In Moonshift: Dinner on the Moon, a young astronaut makes that call. Players explore in 3D, bring ice and soil home, and watch Lumi and Astrocat turn those supplies into water for seedlings and shielding for the crew. The crew needs dinner tomorrow and breathable air today. Later, in MarsShift, dust dims the solar panels and changes how much energy players need to save. We built the game so students can try a plan, see who or what it helps, and explain what had to wait.
details:
The first expedition starts with a bare roof. The player walks out with a scanner, collects six scoops of loose lunar soil, follows the HOME marker and unloads at the station. Back inside, the same soil is on the supply shelf. Give the loader power and Astrocat packs it over the shelter. When a solar particle warning arrives, the roof reduces the crew’s exposure. The fan keeps air moving through the life-support system while the crew waits inside.

A later trip starts with thirsty seedlings. The player brings back crater ice and watches Lumi melt and clean it. Water and electricity for the grow lights move the plants toward the crew’s first harvest. The lab can also use electricity to split clean water and collect oxygen. At each shift, players can preview how their choices change air, water, meals and stored power. A teacher can pause there and ask, “If we give that power to the garden, what will be left for the next shift?”

MarsShift gives the same crew a different problem at Arcadia Station. NASA’s InSight team measured a fall in solar energy from 425 to 275 watt-hours per Martian day during a dust storm. Players face their own version of that decision. When the forecast shows dust, how much power should stay in the battery? NASA’s ice maps also guide the story about searching below the Martian surface. We designed the routes, yields and power units for play.

We built the game with HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Three.js. It runs in a browser with touch or keyboard controls. Short narrated demonstrations show each job, picture controls show the resources it needs, and chapter quizzes ask players to connect what they collected with what it became.
